claim: A loss of the checkpoint kinase ataxia telangiectasia mutated (ATM) leads to impairments in the DNA damage response.
source: A loss of the checkpoint kinase ataxia telangiectasia mutated (ATM) leads to impairments in the DNA damage response, and in humans causes cerebellar neurodegeneration, and an increased risk of cancer.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about ATM function.

claim: A loss of ATM in humans causes cerebellar neurodegeneration.
source: A loss of the checkpoint kinase ataxia telangiectasia mutated (ATM) leads to impairments in the DNA damage response, and in humans causes cerebellar neurodegeneration, and an increased risk of cancer.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about ATM deficiency in humans.

claim: A loss of ATM in humans causes an increased risk of cancer.
source: A loss of the checkpoint kinase ataxia telangiectasia mutated (ATM) leads to impairments in the DNA damage response, and in humans causes cerebellar neurodegeneration, and an increased risk of cancer.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about ATM deficiency in humans.

claim: A loss of ATM is associated with increased protein aggregation.
source: A loss of ATM is also associated with increased protein aggregation.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies in the manuscript.

claim: Targeting ATM results in widespread aggregation of a metastable, disease-associated subfraction of the proteome.
source: Here, we show that targeting ATM, but also ATR or DNA topoisomerases, results in the widespread aggregation of a metastable, disease-associated subfraction of the proteome.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Targeting ATR results in widespread aggregation of a metastable, disease-associated subfraction of the proteome.
source: Here, we show that targeting ATM, but also ATR or DNA topoisomerases, results in the widespread aggregation of a metastable, disease-associated subfraction of the proteome.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Targeting DNA topoisomerases results in widespread aggregation of a metastable, disease-associated subfraction of the proteome.
source: Here, we show that targeting ATM, but also ATR or DNA topoisomerases, results in the widespread aggregation of a metastable, disease-associated subfraction of the proteome.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Huntingtin exon 1 containing an expanded polyglutamine repeat aggregates faster under genotoxic stress conditions.
source: Aggregation-prone model substrates, including Huntingtin exon 1 containing an expanded polyglutamine repeat, aggregate faster under these conditions.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in the manuscript.

claim: The increased aggregation under genotoxic stress results from an overload of chaperone systems.
source: This increased aggregation results from an overload of chaperone systems, which lowers the cell-intrinsic threshold for proteins to aggregate.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data and inference from the results.

claim: Overload of chaperone systems lowers the cell-intrinsic threshold for proteins to aggregate.
source: This increased aggregation results from an overload of chaperone systems, which lowers the cell-intrinsic threshold for proteins to aggregate.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing increased aggregation and chaperone sequestration.

claim: Inhibition of the HSP70 chaperone system exacerbates the increased protein aggregation under genotoxic stress.
source: In line with this, we find that inhibition of the HSP70 chaperone system further exacerbates the increased protein aggregation.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: HSPB5 is a cell-specific suppressor of protein aggregation under genotoxic stress.
source: Moreover, we identify the molecular chaperone HSPB5 as a cell-specific suppressor of it.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing HSPB5 overexpression reduces aggregation in specific cell lines.

claim: Genotoxic conditions trigger widespread protein aggregation in a manner highly reminiscent of aggregation occurring in situations of proteotoxic stress and in proteinopathies.
source: Our findings reveal that various genotoxic conditions trigger widespread protein aggregation in a manner that is highly reminiscent of the aggregation occurring in situations of proteotoxic stress and in proteinopathies.
evidence: This is supported by comparative analysis of aggregating proteins with those found in proteinopathies.

claim: ATM functions as a central regulator of the DNA damage response.
source: The PI3K-like serine/threonine checkpoint kinase ataxia telangiectasia mutated (ATM) functions as a central regulator of the DNA damage response (DDR) and is recruited early to DNA double-strand breaks (DSBs) by the MRE11/RAD50/NBS1 (MRN) complex (Shiloh and Ziv, 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: ATM is recruited early to DNA double-strand breaks by the MRE11/RAD50/NBS1 (MRN) complex.
source: The PI3K-like serine/threonine checkpoint kinase ataxia telangiectasia mutated (ATM) functions as a central regulator of the DNA damage response (DDR) and is recruited early to DNA double-strand breaks (DSBs) by the MRE11/RAD50/NBS1 (MRN) complex (Shiloh and Ziv, 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Defects in ATM give rise to ataxia-telangiectasia (A-T), a multisystem disorder characterized by a predisposition to cancer and progressive neurodegeneration.
source: Defects in ATM give rise to ataxia-telangiectasia (A-T), a multisystem disorder that is characterized by a predisposition to cancer and progressive neurodegeneration (McKinnon, 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Impaired function of ATM has been linked to a disruption of protein homeostasis.
source: Impaired function of ATM has also been linked to a disruption of protein homeostasis and increased protein aggregation (Corcoles-Saez et al., 2018; Lee et al., 2018; Liu et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Protein homeostasis is normally maintained by protein quality control systems, including chaperones and proteolytic pathways.
source: Protein homeostasis is normally maintained by protein quality control systems, including chaperones and proteolytic pathways (Hipp et al., 2019; Labbadia and Morimoto, 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: When the capacity of protein quality control systems becomes overwhelmed during proteotoxic stress, proteins succumb to aggregation more readily.
source: When the capacity of protein quality control systems becomes overwhelmed during (chronic) proteotoxic stress, the stability of the proteome can no longer be sufficiently guarded, causing proteins to succumb to aggregation more readily.
evidence: This is established knowledge about protein homeostasis.

claim: Proteins that are expressed at a relatively high level compared to their intrinsic aggregation propensity (supersaturated proteins) are particularly vulnerable to aggregation.
source: Proteins that are expressed at a relatively high level compared to their intrinsic aggregation propensity, a state referred to as 'supersaturation,' have been shown to be particularly vulnerable in this respect (Ciryam et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: A loss of protein homeostasis and widespread aggregation is associated with a range of degenerative diseases, including neurodegeneration.
source: A loss of protein homeostasis and the accompanying widespread aggregation can have profound consequences, and is associated with a range of (degenerative) diseases, including neurodegeneration (Kampinga and Bergink, 2016; Klaips et al., 2018; Ross and Poirier, 2004).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Loss of MRE11 results in protein aggregation.
source: Loss of MRE11 has recently also been found to result in protein aggregation (Lee et al., 2021), and since MRE11 and ATM function in the same DDR pathway, this raises the question whether other genotoxic conditions can challenge protein homeostasis as well (Ainslie et al., 2021Huiting and Bergink, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a recent study.

claim: Knocking out ATM in U2OS cells results in an increase in protein aggregation.
source: In line with previous findings (Lee et al., 2018), we find that knocking out ATM in both U2OS and HEK293 results in an increase in protein aggregation (Figure 1A and B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in the figures.

claim: Knocking out ATM in HEK293 cells results in an increase in protein aggregation.
source: In line with previous findings (Lee et al., 2018), we find that knocking out ATM in both U2OS and HEK293 results in an increase in protein aggregation (Figure 1A and B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in the figures.

claim: Transient chemical inhibition of ATM results in an increase in aggregated proteins in HEK293T cells.
source: Transient chemical inhibition of ATM (48–72 hr prior to fractionation; Figure 1—figure supplement 1D) resulted in an increase in aggregated proteins in HEK293T cells as well (Figure 1C and D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in the figures.

claim: Chemical inhibition of ATR enhances protein aggregation.
source: This revealed that chemical inhibition of the checkpoint signaling kinase ATR also enhanced protein aggregation (Figure 1C and D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in the figures.

claim: Inhibition of tyrosyl-DNA-phosphodiesterase 1 (TDP1) had no clear effect on protein aggregation.
source: Inhibition of tyrosyl-DNA-phosphodiesterase 1 (TDP1), which repairs various 3′-blocking lesions including topoisomerase 1 (TOP1) cleavage complexes, had no clear effect on protein aggregation (Figure 1C and D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in the figures.

claim: Transient treatment with camptothecin (CPT) causes a strong increase in protein aggregation.
source: Strikingly, we found that transient treatment with either compound caused a particularly strong increase in protein aggregation (Figure 1C and D), which was dose-dependent (Figure 1E and F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in the figures.

claim: Transient treatment with etoposide (Etop) causes a strong increase in protein aggregation.
source: Strikingly, we found that transient treatment with either compound caused a particularly strong increase in protein aggregation (Figure 1C and D), which was dose-dependent (Figure 1E and F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in the figures.

claim: The increase in protein aggregation caused by CPT and etoposide is dose-dependent.
source: Strikingly, we found that transient treatment with either compound caused a particularly strong increase in protein aggregation (Figure 1C and D), which was dose-dependent (Figure 1E and F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in the figures.

claim: The genotoxic impact of CPT and Etop is a consequence of their ability to trap topoisomerase cleavage complexes on the DNA, resulting in DNA damage.
source: The genotoxic impact of CPT and Etop is a well-documented consequence of their ability to trap (i.e., 'poison') respectively TOP1 and TOP2 cleavage complexes on the DNA, resulting in DNA damage (Pommier et al., 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Inhibition of poly(ADP-ribose)polymerases 1–3 (PARP1-3) did not increase aggregation.
source: Inhibition of poly(ADP-ribose)polymerases 1–3 (PARP1-3), involved in single-strand break repair, did not increase aggregation (Figure 1C and D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in the figures.

claim: PARP inhibition reduces the enhanced aggregation triggered by a loss of ATM.
source: Recently, it was reported that PARP inhibition reduces the enhanced aggregation triggered by a loss of ATM (Lee et al., 2021), something we find as well for CPT-treated cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F, G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and citation to previous work.

claim: Neither CPT nor Etop treatment in HEK293T cells had any effect on aggregation within the first 24 hr.
source: Neither CPT nor Etop treatment in HEK293T cells had any effect on aggregation within the first 24 hr (Figure 1G and H).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in the figures.

claim: The increased aggregation occurs only late after genotoxic stress.
source: This reveals that the increased aggregation occurs only late and argues that it does not stem from any immediate, unknown damaging effect of either CPT or Etop on mRNA or protein molecules.
evidence: This is inferred from the time-course experimental data.

claim: The increased protein aggregation triggered by targeting ATM, ATR, and TOPs is a late consequence of genotoxic stress.
source: Together, these data indicate that the increased protein aggregation triggered by targeting ATM, ATR, and TOPs is a late consequence of genotoxic stress.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing time-dependent effects.

claim: 122 proteins aggregated significantly more after CPT treatment compared to control in HEK293T cells.
source: Using a stringent cutoff (Benjamini–Hochberg corrected p<0.05; –1>log2fold change >1; identified in >1 repeats of CPT-treated cells), we determined that 122 proteins aggregated significantly more after CPT treatment compared to only 29 proteins that aggregated less (Figure 2A, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is supported by MS/MS proteomics data.

claim: 29 proteins aggregated significantly less after CPT treatment compared to control in HEK293T cells.
source: Using a stringent cutoff (Benjamini–Hochberg corrected p<0.05; –1>log2fold change >1; identified in >1 repeats of CPT-treated cells), we determined that 122 proteins aggregated significantly more after CPT treatment compared to only 29 proteins that aggregated less (Figure 2A, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is supported by MS/MS proteomics data.

claim: Most proteins that aggregate more after CPT treatment were not identified as aggregating in untreated cells.
source: Most of them were not identified as aggregating in untreated cells, implying that they are soluble under normal conditions.
evidence: This is inferred from the MS/MS proteomics data.

claim: 39 proteins aggregated significantly more in ATM-inhibited HEK293T cells compared to control cells.
source: We detected 39 proteins that aggregated significantly more in ATM-inhibited cells compared to control cells and 5 proteins that aggregated less (Figure 2B, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is supported by MS/MS proteomics data.

claim: 5 proteins aggregated significantly less in ATM-inhibited HEK293T cells compared to control cells.
source: We detected 39 proteins that aggregated significantly more in ATM-inhibited cells compared to control cells and 5 proteins that aggregated less (Figure 2B, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is supported by MS/MS proteomics data.

claim: Only one protein was found to aggregate more after both CPT treatment and inhibition of ATM in HEK293T cells.
source: Surprisingly, only one protein was found to aggregate more after both CPT treatment and inhibition of ATM (Figure 2C), suggesting that these genotoxic conditions drive the aggregation of different proteins.
evidence: This is supported by MS/MS proteomics data.

claim: MCM7, TUBA1A, and HDAC1 aggregate more in CPT-treated HEK293 cells.
source: We selected MCM7, TUBA1A, and HDAC1, three proteins that were identified in our MS/MS analysis, to consistently aggregate more in CPT-treated HEK293T cells but that were not picked up in the ATM inhibition MS/MS analysis and confirmed that all three aggregated more in CPT-treated HEK293 cells (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data.

claim: MCM7, TUBA1A, and HDAC1 aggregate more after treatment of HEK293 cells with ATM inhibitor.
source: MCM7, TUBA1A, and HDAC1 also aggregated more than in unstressed conditions after treatment of HEK293 cells with ATM inhibitor or when ATM was knocked out completely (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data.

claim: MCM7, TUBA1A, and HDAC1 aggregate more in ATM knockout HEK293 cells.
source: MCM7, TUBA1A, and HDAC1 also aggregated more than in unstressed conditions after treatment of HEK293 cells with ATM inhibitor or when ATM was knocked out completely (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data.

claim: 210 proteins aggregated more in ATM KO U2OS cells.
source: We found 210 proteins that aggregated more in ATM KO cells, while 53 proteins aggregated less (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is supported by MS/MS proteomics data.

claim: 53 proteins aggregated less in ATM KO U2OS cells.
source: We found 210 proteins that aggregated more in ATM KO cells, while 53 proteins aggregated less (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is supported by MS/MS proteomics data.

claim: 114 of the 210 proteins that aggregate more in ATM KO U2OS cells were also found to aggregate more in ATM-depleted U2OS cells in a previous study.
source: Of these 210 proteins, 114 were also found to aggregate more in ATM-depleted U2OS cells in a recent study by Lee et al., 2021.
evidence: This is supported by comparison with a cited study.

claim: Treatment of U2OS cells with CPT resulted in 106 proteins aggregating more.
source: Treatment of U2OS cells with CPT resulted in 106 proteins aggregating more and 61 proteins to aggregate less (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is supported by MS/MS proteomics data.

claim: Treatment of U2OS cells with CPT resulted in 61 proteins aggregating less.
source: Treatment of U2OS cells with CPT resulted in 106 proteins aggregating more and 61 proteins to aggregate less (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is supported by MS/MS proteomics data.

claim: Close to 20% of proteins that aggregated more after CPT treatment also aggregated in ATM KO U2OS cells.
source: Close to 20% of proteins that aggregated more after CPT treatment also aggregated in ATM KO U2OS cells (20/106) (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by MS/MS proteomics data.

claim: Proteins that aggregate more in U2OS ATM KO or CPT-treated cells appear to be largely soluble in wild-type cells.
source: Similar to the induced aggregation in HEK293T cells, proteins that aggregate more in U2OS ATM KO or CPT-treated cells appear to be largely soluble in wild-type cells, but now aggregate consistently (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is inferred from the MS/MS proteomics data.

claim: Not a single protein was found to aggregate more in all four different conditions (HEK293T CPT, HEK293T ATM inhibitor, U2OS CPT, U2OS ATM KO).
source: Not a single protein was found to aggregate more in all four different conditions, only two proteins aggregated more in both HEK293T and U2OS cells after CPT treatment, and only one protein overlapped between ATM KO U2OS cells and ATM-inhibited HEK293T cells (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by MS/MS proteomics data.

claim: Cytoskeleton-related GO terms are enriched across the different aggregating proteomes.
source: Cytoskeleton-related terms, including microtubule and microfibril, are enriched across the different aggregating proteomes (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D–F, H).
evidence: This is supported by GO term analysis of the MS/MS data.

claim: Proteins that aggregated more in CPT-treated HEK293T cells are enriched for nucleotide binding terms, most prominently RNA binding.
source: For example, proteins that aggregated more in CPT-treated HEK293T cells are enriched for nucleotide binding terms, most prominently RNA binding, which is highly enriched among proteins that aggregate after ATM inhibition as well (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is supported by GO term analysis of the MS/MS data.

claim: CPT treatment in HEK293T cells drives the aggregation of mitochondrial components.
source: Specifically CPT treatment in HEK293T cells drives the aggregation of mitochondrial components (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by GO term analysis of the MS/MS data.

claim: In U2OS cells, proteins that aggregate more after a loss of ATM or CPT treatment appear to be enriched for components involved in cell-cell contact, including cell adhesion and cellular membrane processes.
source: In U2OS cells, proteins that aggregate more after a loss of ATM or CPT treatment appear to be enriched for components involved in cell-cell contact, including cell adhesion and cellular membrane processes (Figure 2—figure supplement 1F–H).
evidence: This is supported by GO term analysis of the MS/MS data.

claim: 66% (118/179) of the HEK293T baseline aggregating fraction aggregates in the U2OS baseline as well.
source: This revealed that 66% (118/179) of the HEK293T baseline fraction aggregates in the U2OS baseline as well (Figure 2—figure supplement 1J).
evidence: This is supported by MS/MS proteomics data.

claim: 62% (99/160) of the proteins that aggregated more in CPT- or ATM inhibitor-treated HEK293T cells are also part of the U2OS baseline aggregation.
source: Importantly, 62% (99/160) of the proteins that aggregated more in CPT- or ATM inhibitor-treated HEK293T cells are also part of the U2OS baseline (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is supported by MS/MS proteomics data.

claim: In unstressed U2OS cells protein aggregation is substantially more prominent than in untreated HEK293T cells.
source: Indeed, silver staining revealed that in unstressed U2OS cells protein aggregation is substantially more prominent than in untreated HEK293T cells (Figure 2G).
evidence: This is supported by silver staining data.

claim: MCM7, TUBA1A, and HDAC1 all aggregate strongly already in untreated wild-type U2OS cells.
source: This is also reflected in MCM7, TUBA1A, and HDAC1, all three of which aggregate strongly already in (untreated) wild-type U2OS cells (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data.

claim: Aggregated proteins have in general a slightly lower or equal intrinsic propensity to aggregate compared to NIA proteins.
source: Surprisingly, we found that aggregated proteins have in general a slightly lower (for the baseline aggregation) or equal (for CPT- and ATM inhibitor-induced aggregation) intrinsic propensity to aggregate compared to NIA proteins (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by TANGO and CamSol analysis of the MS/MS data.

claim: Proteins that aggregate in CPT- or ATM-inhibited-treated HEK293T cells are in general highly abundant compared to NIA proteins.
source: Interestingly, our MS/MS analysis revealed that proteins that aggregate in CPT- or ATM-inhibited-treated HEK293T cells are in general highly abundant compared to NIA proteins in (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by MS/MS proteomics data.

claim: Genes coding for the aggregating proteins are in general higher expressed than genes coding for NIA proteins.
source: After performing RNA sequencing on the same HEK293T cell samples that we used for our MS/MS analysis (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, Supplementary file 2), we found that genes coding for the aggregating proteins are in general higher expressed than genes coding for NIA proteins (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by RNA sequencing data.

claim: Aggregating proteins are in general more supersaturated than NIA proteins.
source: Using the RNA-sequencing data (Supplementary file 2), we confirmed that aggregating proteins are in general indeed more supersaturated than NIA proteins (Figure 3D–F).
evidence: This is supported by supersaturation analysis using RNA-seq and TANGO data.

claim: Most supersaturated proteins did not become SDS-insoluble, even after treatment with CPT or ATM inhibition.
source: Although the relative supersaturation of aggregating proteins in HEK293T cells is intriguing, our data also indicates that most supersaturated proteins did not become SDS-insoluble, even after treatment with CPT or ATM inhibition (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is inferred from the supersaturation analysis.

claim: HEK293T baseline aggregation and both CPT- and ATM inhibitor-induced aggregation are made up of proteins that have a higher average LLPS propensity than NIA proteins.
source: Using catGRANULE (Mitchell et al., 2013; http://tartaglialab.com), we find that HEK293T baseline aggregation and both CPT- and ATM inhibitor-induced aggregation are indeed made up of proteins that have a higher average LLPS propensity than NIA proteins (Figure 3G).
evidence: This is supported by catGRANULE analysis of the MS/MS data.

claim: HEK293T baseline and ATM inhibitor-induced aggregation are enriched for proteins that have a high propensity to engage in LLPS-relevant pi-pi interactions.
source: HEK293T baseline and ATM inhibitor-induced aggregation are also enriched for proteins that have a high propensity to engage in LLPS-relevant pi-pi interactions, as indicated by both a higher average PScore and a larger percentage of proteins that have a PScore > 4 (i.e., above the threshold defined by Vernon et al., 2018; Figure 3—figure supplement 1D and E).
evidence: This is supported by PScore analysis of the MS/MS data.

claim: Baseline aggregation in U2OS cells is made up of supersaturated, LLPS-prone proteins.
source: Upon examining the proteins that aggregate in U2OS cells, we found further support for this. Baseline aggregation in U2OS cells is also made up of supersaturated, LLPS-prone proteins (Figure 3—figure supplement 1H–R).
evidence: This is supported by supersaturation and LLPS propensity analysis of the MS/MS data.

claim: Many supersaturated proteins are not SDS-insoluble in U2OS cells, even in cells treated with CPT or in cells lacking ATM.
source: Despite the baseline aggregation being far more pronounced in U2OS cells than in HEK293T cells, many supersaturated proteins are not SDS-insoluble in U2OS cells, even in cells treated with CPT or in cells lacking ATM (Figure 3—figure supplement 1O).
evidence: This is inferred from the supersaturation analysis.

claim: Proteins that aggregate more in U2OS ATM KO cells are supersaturated compared to U2OS NIA proteins.
source: In U2OS ATM KO cells, proteins that aggregate more are supersaturated compared to U2OS NIA proteins (Figure 3—figure supplement 1M); for CPT-treated cells, this is not the case (Figure 3—figure supplement 1M–O).
evidence: This is supported by supersaturation analysis of the MS/MS data.

claim: Proteins that aggregate more in U2OS ATM KO cells have a higher general propensity to engage in LLPS as predicted by PScore and catGRANULE.
source: Proteins that aggregate more in U2OS ATM KO cells also have a higher general propensity to engage in LLPS as predicted by PScore and catGRANULE (Figure 3—figure supplement 1P and Q), while proteins that aggregate more in CPT-treated cells are enriched for proteins with a PScore > 4 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1R).
evidence: This is supported by PScore and catGRANULE analysis of the MS/MS data.

claim: Only two transcripts were significantly altered after ATM inhibition in HEK293T cells despite the enhanced aggregation occurring in these cells.
source: Intriguingly, only two transcripts (one up and one down) were significantly altered (–1 > log2FC > 1) after ATM inhibition in HEK293T cells despite the enhanced aggregation occurring in these cells.
evidence: This is supported by RNA sequencing data.

claim: The enhanced aggregation after CPT treatment or a loss of ATM function is mostly driven by the physicochemical characteristics of the proteins involved.
source: This further underlines that the enhanced aggregation after CPT treatment or a loss of ATM function is mostly driven by the physicochemical characteristics of the proteins involved.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of transcriptional changes and the supersaturation/LLPS propensity data.

claim: The consistent aggregation of vulnerable proteins across independent repeats argues against the possibility that this is caused by any genotoxic stress-induced DNA sequence alterations in their own coding regions.
source: Their consistent aggregation across independent repeats argues against the possibility that this is caused by any genotoxic stress-induced DNA sequence alterations in their own coding regions as these would occur more randomly throughout the genome.
evidence: This is inferred from the consistency of the MS/MS data.

claim: The increased aggregation cannot be explained by any changes in abundance of the proteins involved.
source: Moreover, we find that the increased aggregation can also not be explained by any changes in abundance of the proteins involved, resulting for example from DNA damage-induced transcriptional dysregulation, as very limited overlap exists between proteins that aggregate and proteins with an altered expression upon CPT treatment or ATM loss (see Figure 4A for HEK293T and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A for U2OS).
evidence: This is supported by comparison of MS/MS and RNA-seq data.

claim: A long-term consequence of genotoxic conditions is a global lowering of the aggregation threshold of proteins.
source: Instead, our data indicate that a long-term consequence of these genotoxic conditions is a global lowering of the aggregation threshold of proteins.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing widespread aggregation of metastable proteins.

claim: Proteins that aggregate more in HEK293T and U2OS cells after CPT treatment or after a loss of ATM are enriched for proteins that have been reported to aggregate upon heat treatment of cells.
source: In line with this, we find that proteins that aggregate more in HEK293T and U2OS cells after CPT treatment or after a (functional) loss of ATM are enriched for proteins that have been reported to aggregate upon heat treatment of cells (Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1C; Mymrikov et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by comparison with a cited heat stress aggregation dataset.

claim: Proteins that aggregate more after genotoxic stress are enriched for constituents of stress granules.
source: In addition, they are enriched for constituents of stress granules (Figure 4C, Figure 4—figure supplement 1D; http://rnagranuledb.lunenfeld.ca), cellular condensates that have been found to function as nucleation sites for protein aggregation (Dobra et al., 2018; Mateju et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by comparison with a stress granule database and citations.

claim: Protein synthesis is reduced approximately threefold in CPT-treated cells.
source: Notably, protein synthesis is reduced approximately threefold in CPT-treated cells (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by radioactive pulse labeling data.

claim: Radioactively labeled proteins were present in the aggregating fraction of CPT-treated cells but were not enriched compared to control cells.
source: Despite this strong reduction in protein synthesis, radioactively labeled proteins were still clearly present in the aggregating fraction of CPT-treated cells. They were however not enriched in the aggregating fraction compared to control cells (Figure 4D), indicating that the enhanced aggregation triggered by CPT is not explained through an accelerated aggregation of specifically newly synthesized proteins.
evidence: This is supported by radioactive pulse labeling data.

claim: Proteins that aggregate after transient CPT treatment are enriched for constituents of various disease-associated protein aggregates.
source: Intriguingly, we find that proteins that aggregate after transient CPT treatment are enriched for constituents of various disease-associated protein aggregates (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is supported by comparison with disease-associated aggregation datasets.

claim: 67% (82/122) of proteins that aggregate after CPT treatment have been previously identified in TDP-43 aggregates, Lewy bodies, α-synuclein-induced aggregates, or found to aggregate in Huntington's disease or Alzheimer's disease brains.
source: 67% (82/122) of them – or their mouse homologs – have already previously been identified in TDP-43 aggregates (Dammer et al., 2012; Zuo et al., 2021), Lewy bodies (McCormack et al., 2019), or α-synuclein-induced aggregates (Mahul-Mellier et al., 2020), or found to aggregate in Huntington's disease (HD) (Hosp et al., 2017) or Alzheimer's disease (AD) brains (Hales et al., 2016; Kepchia et al., 2020 Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by comparison with cited disease-associated aggregation datasets.

claim: Transient targeting of ATM, ATR, and TOPs accelerates polyQ aggregation in HEK293 cells.
source: Transient targeting of ATM, ATR, and in particular TOPs, but not TDP1, 24–48 hr prior to the expression of polyQ (Figure 4—figure supplement 1F) indeed accelerated polyQ aggregation in these cells (Figure 4F, Figure 4—figure supplement 1G), closely mirroring the increased aggregation that we observed before (Figure 1C and D).
evidence: This is supported by filter trap assay data.

claim: The accelerated polyQ aggregation under genotoxic conditions is dose-dependent.
source: The accelerated polyQ aggregation under these conditions is also dose-dependent (Figure 4G, Figure 4—figure supplement 1H and I), and it is not explained by changes in total polyQ levels (Figure 4—figure supplement 1G–I).
evidence: This is supported by filter trap assay and Western blot data.

claim: The accelerated polyQ aggregation induced by genotoxic conditions cannot be explained by an exacerbated repeat instability.
source: Importantly, we find no evidence that the accelerated polyQ aggregation induced by these genotoxic conditions can be explained by an exacerbated repeat instability (Figure 4—figure supplement 1J).
evidence: This is supported by CAG repeat length analysis data.

claim: Transient targeting of either ATM or TOP1 results in an enrichment of luciferase-GFP in the aggregated fraction.
source: We find that transient targeting of either ATM or TOP1 results in an enrichment of luciferase-GFP in the aggregated fraction (Figure 4H).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data.

claim: ATM inhibition and CPT treatment result in increased aggregation of multiple (co)chaperones in HEK293T cells.
source: We noted that ATM inhibition and in particular CPT treatment resulted in an increased aggregation of multiple (co)chaperones in HEK293T cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This is supported by MS/MS proteomics data.

claim: In U2OS cells, many (co)chaperones are already aggregating regardless of exposure to genotoxic stress.
source: In U2OS cells, many (co)chaperones are already aggregating regardless of exposure to genotoxic stress, but still several chaperones aggregated significantly more in ATM KO cells or in cells treated with CPT (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C and D).
evidence: This is supported by MS/MS proteomics data.

claim: HSPA8 and HSPA1A clients are enriched among aggregating proteins.
source: Upon cross-referencing the NIA and aggregating fractions against a recently generated client database of HSPA8 (HSC70; constitutively active form of HSP70) and HSPA1A (constitutively active and stress-inducible HSP70) (Ryu et al., 2020), we find that HSPA8 and HSPA1A clients are enriched among aggregating proteins (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by comparison with a cited client database.

claim: All aggregating fractions are enriched for (co)chaperone interactors compared to nonaggregating proteins.
source: We find that all aggregating fractions are enriched for (co)chaperone interactors compared to nonaggregating proteins (NIA) (Figure 5C, Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by BioGRID interaction database analysis.

claim: Treatment with CPT results in an overall upward shift of (co)chaperone expression levels in HEK293T cells.
source: In HEK293T cells, we find that treatment with CPT results in an overall upward shift of (co)chaperone expression levels, as measured in both our WCL MS/MS analysis (16 up, 8 down) (Figure 5E) and in our RNAseq dataset (11 up, 5 down) (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is supported by MS/MS and RNA-seq data.

claim: HSF1 is partially activated by CPT treatment in HEK293T cells.
source: HSF1 is indeed partially activated by CPT treatment in HEK293T cells (Figure 5G).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data showing HSF1 phosphorylation.

claim: ATM inhibition in HEK293T cells resulted in a marginal HSF1 activation.
source: ATM inhibition in HEK293T cells resulted in a marginal HSF1 activation.
evidence: This is inferred from the Western blot data.

claim: Gene expression levels of Clusterin (CLU) are >100-fold higher in wild-type U2OS compared to HEK293T cells.
source: For example, we found that gene expression levels of the small heat shock-like protein Clusterin (CLU) are >100-fold higher in wild-type U2OS compared to HEK293T cells, gene expression levels of the stress-inducible HSPA1A are >150-fold higher, and that of HSPB5 (or CRYAB, i.e., αB-crystallin) were >400-fold higher.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data.

claim: Gene expression levels of HSPA1A are >150-fold higher in wild-type U2OS compared to HEK293T cells.
source: For example, we found that gene expression levels of the small heat shock-like protein Clusterin (CLU) are >100-fold higher in wild-type U2OS compared to HEK293T cells, gene expression levels of the stress-inducible HSPA1A are >150-fold higher, and that of HSPB5 (or CRYAB, i.e., αB-crystallin) were >400-fold higher.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data.

claim: Gene expression levels of HSPB5 are >400-fold higher in wild-type U2OS compared to HEK293T cells.
source: For example, we found that gene expression levels of the small heat shock-like protein Clusterin (CLU) are >100-fold higher in wild-type U2OS compared to HEK293T cells, gene expression levels of the stress-inducible HSPA1A are >150-fold higher, and that of HSPB5 (or CRYAB, i.e., αB-crystallin) were >400-fold higher.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data.

claim: Mild HSP70 inhibition using VER-155008 after CPT treatment increased CPT-induced protein aggregation.
source: Indeed, mild HSP70 inhibition using the HSP70/HSC70 inhibitor VER-155008 after CPT treatment increased CPT-induced protein aggregation even further, while having no clear impact on aggregation in control cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by silver staining data.

claim: Overexpression of HSPB5 drastically reduced the enhanced protein aggregation in U2OS ATM KO cells.
source: We generated U2OS cells that stably overexpress HSPB5 in both wild-type and ATM-deficient backgrounds (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C), and confirmed that this drastically reduced the enhanced protein aggregation in the latter (Figure 6B and C).
evidence: This is supported by silver staining and quantification data.

claim: HSPB5 overexpression reduced ProteoStat aggresome staining in U2OS ATM KO cells.
source: HSPB5 overexpression also reduced ProteoStat aggresome staining and the occurrence of cytoplasmic FUS puncta (without affecting overall FUS levels; see Supplementary file 1), two other markers of a disrupted protein homeostasis (Figure 6D–G; Neumann et al., 2006; Shen et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data.

claim: HSPB5 overexpression reduced the occurrence of cytoplasmic FUS puncta in U2OS ATM KO cells.
source: HSPB5 overexpression also reduced ProteoStat aggresome staining and the occurrence of cytoplasmic FUS puncta (without affecting overall FUS levels; see Supplementary file 1), two other markers of a disrupted protein homeostasis (Figure 6D–G; Neumann et al., 2006; Shen et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data.

claim: Gamma irradiation-induced DNA lesion accumulation and subsequent resolution as measured by 53BP1 foci formation was not affected by HSPB5 expression in U2OS wild-type or ATM KO cells.
source: However, we found no indication for this as the gamma irradiation-induced DNA lesion accumulation and subsequent resolution as measured by 53BP1 foci formation was not affected by HSPB5 expression in neither U2OS wild-type nor ATM KO cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 1D and E).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data.

claim: Neither HSPB5, nor HSP70 nor HSP90 accumulated at CPT- or gamma irradiation-induced DNA damage sites.
source: Moreover, neither HSPB5, nor HSP70 nor HSP90 accumulated at either CPT- or gamma irradiation-induced DNA damage sites (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A–C).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data.

claim: The overload of chaperones is not due to a sequestering to DNA damage sites.
source: This points out that the overload of chaperones is not due to a sequestering to DNA damage sites.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of chaperone accumulation at DNA damage sites.

claim: Overexpression of HSPB5 can reduce the enhanced protein aggregation in CPT-treated U2OS cells.
source: Crucially, we found that overexpression of HSPB5 can reduce the enhanced protein aggregation in CPT-treated U2OS cells as well (Figure 6H, I), but that stable overexpression of HSPB5 has no effect on the CPT-induced aggregation in HEK293 cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: This is supported by silver staining data.

claim: Stable overexpression of HSPB5 has no effect on the CPT-induced aggregation in HEK293 cells.
source: Crucially, we found that overexpression of HSPB5 can reduce the enhanced protein aggregation in CPT-treated U2OS cells as well (Figure 6H, I), but that stable overexpression of HSPB5 has no effect on the CPT-induced aggregation in HEK293 cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: This is supported by silver staining data.

claim: TOP poisoning and functional impairment of ATM or ATR trigger a widespread aggregation of LLPS-prone and supersaturated proteins.
source: Here, we report that TOP poisoning and functional impairment of ATM or ATR trigger a widespread aggregation of LLPS-prone and supersaturated proteins.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data.

claim: The aggregation of metastable proteins is a consequence of an overload of chaperone systems under genotoxic conditions.
source: Our data show that the aggregation of these metastable proteins is a consequence of an overload of chaperone systems under these genotoxic conditions.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data and inference.

claim: CPT treatment leads to a strong reduction in protein synthesis over time.
source: It is further supported by the notion that CPT treatment leads to a strong reduction in protein synthesis over time, something that has been reported for other forms of DNA damage as well (Halim et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and citation.

claim: Reduced protein synthesis is a well-known response to proteotoxic stress and is believed to lower the strong demand for chaperone capacity of nascent chains.
source: Reduced protein synthesis is a well-known response to proteotoxic stress and is believed to lower the strong demand for chaperone capacity of nascent chains that are innately vulnerable to misfolding and aggregation (Balchin et al., 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Despite a reduction in protein synthesis, genotoxic stress still leads to an overload of chaperone systems.
source: This indicates that despite a reduction in protein synthesis, genotoxic stress still leads to an overload of chaperone systems, causing protein homeostasis to shift.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing reduced synthesis but increased aggregation.

claim: The shift in protein homeostasis after genotoxic stress is reminiscent of what occurs under conditions of chronic stress.
source: The observed shift in protein homeostasis after genotoxic stress is strikingly reminiscent of what is believed to occur under conditions of (chronic) stress (Weids et al., 2016) and during many age-related neurodegenerative disorders (David et al., 2010; Hipp et al., 2019; Morley et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by comparison with cited literature.

claim: Supersaturated proteins have been found to be overrepresented in cellular pathways associated with neurodegenerative disorders.
source: Supersaturated proteins have been found to be overrepresented in cellular pathways associated with these disorders (Ciryam et al., 2015), and disease-associated aggregating proteins, including FUS, tau, and α-synuclein, are known to exhibit LLPS behavior (reviewed in Zbinden et al., 2020).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The shift in protein homeostasis under genotoxic stress conditions can be caused by either an altered capacity of protein quality control systems or by an increased demand emanating from an altered proteome.
source: The shift in protein homeostasis under genotoxic stress conditions can theoretically be caused by either an altered capacity of protein quality control systems or by an increased demand emanating from an altered proteome.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about possible mechanisms.

claim: The overload of chaperone systems is largely caused by an increased demand for chaperone activity in the proteome.
source: Nevertheless, our data lead us to hypothesize that the overload of chaperone systems is largely caused by an increased demand for chaperone activity in the proteome.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the experimental data.

claim: The strong upregulation of several small heat shock proteins in U2OS cells points at a rewiring of the chaperone network towards a more prominent reliance on this class of chaperones.
source: The strong upregulation of several small heat shock (-like) proteins in U2OS cells, including HSPB5, seems to point at a rewiring of the chaperone network in this cell line towards a more prominent reliance on this class of chaperones.
evidence: This is inferred from the RNA-seq data showing differential chaperone expression.

claim: Cancer cells inherently exhibit elevated levels of protein stress, which has been attributed to an increased protein folding and degradation demand.
source: Cancer cells inherently exhibit elevated levels of protein stress, which has been attributed to an increased protein folding and degradation demand (Dai et al., 2012; Deshaies, 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Any increased demand caused by genotoxic conditions is independent of quantitative changes of the aggregating proteins themselves and likely also of any genetic alterations in their coding regions.
source: Our data indicate that any increased demand caused by these genotoxic conditions is, however independent of quantitative changes of the aggregating proteins themselves and likely also of any genetic alterations in their coding regions (in cis genetic alterations).
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of correlation between aggregation and protein/transcript abundance changes.

claim: During proteomic stress a destabilization of the background proteome can result in a competition for the limited chaperone capacity available.
source: Previous studies have shown that during proteomic stress a destabilization of the background proteome can result in a competition for the limited chaperone capacity available, causing proteins that are highly dependent on chaperones for their stability and solubility to aggregate readily (Gidalevitz et al., 2010; Gidalevitz et al., 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The aggregation that occurs after genotoxic stress is enriched for RNA-binding proteins.
source: Strikingly, we find that the aggregation that occurs after genotoxic stress is enriched for RNA-binding proteins.
evidence: This is supported by GO term analysis of the MS/MS data.

claim: The enhanced aggregation after genotoxic stress can be mitigated by inhibiting PARylation.
source: This enhanced aggregation can also be mitigated by inhibiting PARylation, which plays a key role in the regulation of LLPS processes (Duan et al., 2019; McGurk et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and citations.

claim: Aberrant LLPS can drive the nucleation of insoluble protein aggregates.
source: LLPS is a different biochemical process than protein aggregation (with different underlying mechanisms and principles), but aberrant LLPS can drive the nucleation of insoluble (fibrillar) protein aggregates, for example, for polyQ (Peskett et al., 2018).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Chaperones, and in particular small heat shock proteins, play a pivotal role in the surveillance of biomolecular condensates.
source: Although data is so far limited, chaperones, and in particular small heat shock proteins, have been reported to play a pivotal role in the surveillance of biomolecular condensates.
evidence: This is established knowledge from the literature.

claim: The HSPB8-BAG3-HSPA1A complex is important for maintaining stress granule dynamics.
source: For example, the HSPB8-BAG3-HSPA1A complex has been found to be important for maintaining stress granule dynamics (Ganassi et al., 2016), and recent work uncovered that HSPB1 is important to prevent aberrant phase transitions of FUS (Liu et al., 2020).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: HSPB1 is important to prevent aberrant phase transitions of FUS.
source: For example, the HSPB8-BAG3-HSPA1A complex has been found to be important for maintaining stress granule dynamics (Ganassi et al., 2016), and recent work uncovered that HSPB1 is important to prevent aberrant phase transitions of FUS (Liu et al., 2020).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: HSPB5 has been found to associate with nuclear speckles.
source: Interestingly, although HSPB5 itself has so far not been shown to undergo LLPS, like HSPB1, it has been found to associate with nuclear speckles (van den IJssel et al., 1998), which are membraneless as well.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: HSPB5 is important to maintain the stability of the cytoskeleton.
source: HSPB5 has also been shown to be important to maintain the stability of the cytoskeleton (Ghosh et al., 2007; Golenhofen et al., 1999; Yin et al., 2019), and we find that many proteins that aggregate upon genotoxic stress conditions are cytoskeleton (-related) components.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Cytoskeleton organization is regulated through LLPS processes.
source: A growing body of evidence indicates that cytoskeleton organization is regulated through LLPS processes (reviewed in Wiegand and Hyman, 2020).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Genotoxic stress conditions can exacerbate the risk of aberrant progression of LLPS processes.
source: Our data thus indicate that genotoxic stress conditions can exacerbate the risk of aberrant progression of LLPS processes, which in turn may trigger an overload of chaperone systems.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing LLPS-prone protein aggregation.

claim: The increased protein aggregation that occurs after a loss of ATM has been recently attributed to an accumulation of DNA damage.
source: The increased protein aggregation that occurs after a loss of ATM – including in A-T patient brains – has been recently attributed to an accumulation of DNA damage (Lee et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a recent study.

claim: An impaired response to DNA damage is believed to be the primary driving force of A-T phenotypes.
source: As an impaired response to DNA damage is believed to be the primary driving force of A-T phenotypes (Shiloh, 2020), these findings have fueled the idea that a disruption of protein homeostasis may be an important disease mechanism in A-T.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: The widespread aggregation caused by a loss of ATM follows a predictable pattern that overlaps with the aggregation believed to underlie many neurodegenerative disorders.
source: Our data provide further support for this as they show that the widespread aggregation caused by a loss of ATM follows a predictable pattern that overlaps strikingly with the aggregation that is believed to underlie many neurodegenerative disorders.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data showing overlap with disease-associated aggregation.

claim: Other genotoxic conditions, including chemotherapeutic TOP poisons, can have a very similar impact on protein aggregation as loss of ATM.
source: Importantly, our findings also provide a proof of principle that other genotoxic conditions – including chemotherapeutic TOP poisons – can have a very similar impact.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data showing similar aggregation patterns.

claim: There exists a broader link between DNA damage and a loss of protein homeostasis.
source: This points at the existence of a broader link between DNA damage and a loss of protein homeostasis .
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing multiple genotoxic conditions trigger aggregation.
